newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lawyers ask whether Iran "Fatwa" justified murder.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers ask whether Iran "Fatwa" justified murder.

text.p: A Berlin trial in which prosecutors have accused Iran's leaders of the murder of Kurdish dissidents was delayed on Thursday when the defence asked Islamic experts to testify on religious law.

In the midst of their closing remarks in the three-year trial, lawyers defending an Iranian and four Lebanese unexpectedly called a witness to take the stand and requested another Islamic expert testify next week.

Heinz Halm from Tuebingen University was asked to testify on the possibility that Iran's spiritual leaders had placed a "Fatwa" or religious edict on the victims such as that placed on British author Salman Rushdie.
Iran's late leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa against Rushdie in 1989, ordering his killing for alleged blasphemy against Islam in his book "The Satanic Verses".

Lawyers asked whether Lebanese Abbas Rhayel, charged with gunning the men down, could have been acting under a Fatwa and asked Halm whether as a devout Moslem the accused had any choice but to obey such a ruling.
Halm told the court that a Fatwa was a directive but not a command and therefore no one was obliged to act on it.

It was yet another delay in the trial that has soured diplomatic relations between Bonn and Tehran over prosecutors' accusations Iran's leaders ordered the gangland-style assassination in Berlin to stamp on its political opponents.

The trial for the 1992 murder of three Kurdish dissidents and their interpretor in a Berlin restaurant was due to wind up this month, but with the latest delay the verdict was not now expected until April.

Prosecutors have accused Rhayel and suspected leader of the commando, Iranian Kazem Darabi, of murder and demanded life sentences in jail for them. They have accused the other three of complicity to murder demanding five to eleven years jail.
